title: A handful of leaves
hook: the Buddha holds a few leaves: what I have taught is this; what I know is the forest; I taught what helps (SN 56.31)

segments.voice: Yesterday: three turns and twelve aspects, the Buddha's own checklist. Your line: no claim until all twelve are clear.
screen: `THREE TURNS — NO CLAIM UNTIL ALL TWELVE ARE CLEAR.`

segments.voice: A cook copies out a family recipe on the back of an envelope: five ingredients, three steps. She knows far more: the history of the dish, why the onions go in first, the aunt who taught her. She leaves it out on purpose, because the friend holding the envelope needs to make dinner tonight. The handful of leaves came up briefly on the last day of year one. Today it's back in its home, the book of the Connected Discourses on the four truths, read slowly: the setting, the full list of reasons, and the test it leaves behind.
screen: `A RECIPE ON AN ENVELOPE.` → `SHE LEAVES THE REST OUT.` → `READ IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: The Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi. He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, these in my hand or the leaves in the grove overhead? The leaves in the grove, they say, by far. In the same way, he says, the things I have directly known but not taught are far more. Then the part that's easy to skip. Why hasn't he taught them? Because they aren't beneficial. They don't belong to the basics of the holy life. They don't lead to letting go, to calm, to peace, to direct knowing, to awakening, to nibbana. And what has he taught? This is dukkha. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Because that does help. It leads to letting go, to calm, to peace, to awakening. So the handful isn't a random sample. It's a careful choice, and the filter is simple: does it help? The Buddha isn't hiding anything mysterious behind his back, or saying the rest of the forest is forbidden. He's a teacher who knows what a student needs, the way the cook knows her friend needs dinner. Fittingly, this sutta sits in the book of the four truths, the Buddha explaining why the last two weeks have been about four sentences and not four hundred. And it hands us a test for anything we read, watch, or worry about: does this lead to calm and freedom, or just to more noise?
screen: `WHICH ARE MORE?` · `WHY NOT THE FOREST?` · `WHAT'S IN THE HAND.` · `THE FILTER: DOES IT HELP?` · then, large: `ONLY WHAT HELPS.`

segments.voice: Hold a few leaves loosely in your open palm, or anything small, a few coins or dried beans, and feel how little they weigh. Then, breathing slowly, let your mind fill with everything you're carrying today: plans, news, worries. For each one, ask quietly: is this in the handful, or is it the forest?
Simsapa. The grove of trees where the Buddha held up a handful of leaves, teaching only what helps toward calm and freedom.
Your line: only what helps. Four sentences, chosen with care, out of a whole forest. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of the simsapa leaves to explain why the teaching centers on the four noble truths and on what leads to peace, rather than on every question that can be asked.

fork.setup: you're a monk in the simsapa grove. the Buddha says he knows far more than he's taught. why, he asks, hasn't he taught it?
options: because you aren't ready for secrets.
because it doesn't help toward peace and awakening.
fork.reveal: he says the rest isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to letting go, calm, peace and nibbana; the four truths do.

original.note: Pali siṃsapā: the simsapa tree (often identified as Indian rosewood), whose grove gives the sutta its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the handful of leaves means the Buddha kept secrets.
what it means: he chose to teach only what helps toward freedom, and named it: the four truths.

what a scholar hears: SN 56.31 sits in the Saccasaṃyutta, the connected sayings on the truths; its list, nibbidā, virāga, nirodha, upasama, abhiññā, sambodhi, nibbāna, recurs in other suttas as the test of what is worth teaching.

chat.says: Why did the Buddha say he only taught a handful of leaves?
options: He chose only what helps: what leads to calm, peace and awakening.
The rest of what he knew was forbidden for anyone to think about.
A handful was all he had learned before he started teaching.
chat.meaning: In the simsapa grove, the Buddha said what he knew but didn't teach was far more; he taught the four truths because they lead to awakening.

simsapa.meaning: a kind of tree; its grove gives the sutta its name

Kosambi.meaning: an old Indian city near the simsapa grove

nibbana.meaning: blowing out: the ending of greed, hatred and delusion

dukkha.meaning: suffering, unease, the pain that comes with life

Connected Discourses.meaning: a large collection of the Buddha's talks, grouped by topic
